title: Right vs. Right — 10 Impossible Dilemmas
theme: Ethical dilemmas where both sides have valid moral arguments
description: What happens when both choices are right? Over 10 rounds, you'll face genuine ethical dilemmas — truth vs. loyalty, individual vs. community, justice vs. mercy. No trick answers. No obvious villains. Just you, your values, and impossible choices.
learning_objectives: Recognize that ethical dilemmas often involve two valid moral principles in conflict
Develop the ability to reason through moral complexity without defaulting to simple answers
Understand your own moral framework and where your values guide your decisions
how_to_play: Each round presents a dilemma where both options are morally defensible. There are no wrong answers. Choose what feels right to you and read the reflection. The goal isn't to score — it's to understand how you think about right and wrong.

glossary_terms.definition: A situation where you must choose between two morally valid but conflicting options
The process of thinking through what's right and wrong, considering consequences and principles
The idea that the right action is the one that produces the most good for the most people
The idea that some actions are right or wrong regardless of their consequences — following rules and duties
The willingness to act on your values even when it's difficult, unpopular, or risky

rounds.title: Truth vs. Loyalty
rounds.situation: {player_name}, your best friend Meera confides that she lied on her college application — she listed a volunteering programme she never actually completed. She got accepted to her dream college partly because of it. She trusts you with this secret. Then the college calls you as a reference and directly asks: 'Did Meera participate in the community service programme she mentioned?'
rounds.story: Truth demands you answer honestly. Loyalty demands you protect your friend. Both are moral principles.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian teenager on a phone call looking torn, friend's photo and college admission letter visible in background
rounds.coaching_moment: When truth and loyalty collide, there's no clean exit — only the choice that you can live with.

choices.label: Tell the truth
choices.description: Say, 'I'm not sure about that specific programme.' You don't lie, but you don't confirm her claim either.
choices.consequence_hint: You protect your integrity and the college gets honest information, but Meera's dream may unravel — and she'll know it was you

events.description: The college investigates. Meera's admission is put on hold. She calls you crying: 'You were the only one who knew.'

choices.label: Protect your friend
choices.description: Confirm the volunteering. Meera made a mistake, but losing her college spot seems like a disproportionate punishment.
choices.consequence_hint: You save Meera's dream but compromise your own honesty — and the college is making a decision based on false information

events.description: Meera gets into college. She hugs you. But every time she mentions the volunteering on campus, something in your stomach turns.

choices.label: Refuse to answer the question
choices.description: Tell the college, 'I'd prefer not to comment on specific activities. Meera is a wonderful person.' Neither lie nor confirm.
choices.consequence_hint: You avoid the direct conflict, but your non-answer itself is a kind of answer — and the college may read between the lines

events.description: The college interviewer pauses. 'That's... an interesting way to put it.' They don't push further, but they make a note.

expert_pick.reason: Ethical decision-making builds lasting trust — the foundation of all leadership.

rounds.title: Individual vs. Community
rounds.situation: {player_name}, your family owns a small plot of land in your village. The government wants to build a public hospital on it — it would serve 50,000 people who currently travel 40 km for healthcare. They'll pay fair compensation, but this land has been in your family for three generations. Your grandmother planted the mango trees. Your father was born there. The family is divided.
rounds.story: Individual rights and community needs — both are sacred in a democracy. When they collide, what wins?
rounds.image_prompt: Indian family standing on ancestral farmland with old mango trees, hospital blueprint visible in government official's hand
rounds.coaching_moment: There's no formula for weighing one family's heritage against fifty thousand people's healthcare. That's what makes it a genuine dilemma.

choices.label: Agree to give the land
choices.description: 50,000 people need healthcare. Your sacrifice serves the greater good. Accept the compensation and let the hospital be built.
choices.consequence_hint: You help an entire community but lose something irreplaceable — family history can't be compensated with money

events.description: Your grandmother cries. But at the hospital inauguration three years later, a mother thanks you: 'My son was born safely because of this hospital.'

choices.label: Refuse — the land is yours
choices.description: Property rights exist for a reason. The government can find another plot. Your family's connection to this land is not for sale.
choices.consequence_hint: You protect your family's heritage, but 50,000 people continue to travel 40 km for basic healthcare

events.description: Your grandmother is relieved. The hospital is eventually built 3 years later on another plot, further away. Some patients don't survive the extra distance.

choices.label: Negotiate conditions
choices.description: Agree, but demand: name the hospital after your grandmother, preserve the mango trees in the courtyard, and guarantee your family free healthcare for life.
choices.consequence_hint: Creative compromise that honours both values — but some will say you're profiting from a sacrifice

events.description: The hospital is named 'Kamala Devi Memorial Hospital.' The mango trees stand in the courtyard. Patients sit under them while waiting.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Short-Term vs. Long-Term
rounds.situation: Your father runs a small printing press, {player_name}. Business is failing — they've lost half their customers to digital. Your father can't afford your Class 12 coaching fees (₹60,000). You've been offered a job at a local shop for ₹8,000/month. If you work full-time, you can pay for coaching yourself. But working full-time means you can't study properly. Your boards are in 5 months.
rounds.story: Work now and fund your education, or study now and risk not affording it. Short-term sacrifice vs. long-term investment.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian teenager looking at coaching centre brochure and a job offer letter, father's worried face in background, printing press visible
rounds.coaching_moment: The hardest trade-offs are the ones where both the short-term need and the long-term goal are completely real.

choices.label: Take the job — pay for coaching
choices.description: Work, earn, and pay your own way. Study late at night. Sacrifice sleep but maintain dignity.
choices.consequence_hint: You fund your education independently, but exhaustion may hurt your board exam scores — the very thing you're paying for

events.description: You work 8 hours and study 4. Your grades dip but don't collapse. Your father's eyes show both pride and guilt.

choices.label: Focus on studies — find another way to pay
choices.description: Don't work. Find scholarships, ask coaching centres for fee waivers, borrow from relatives if needed. Protect study time.
choices.consequence_hint: You protect your future, but the borrowing and asking creates its own burdens — financial and emotional

events.description: You get a partial fee waiver. Your uncle lends ₹20,000. Your boards go well. But the debt weighs on your family.

choices.label: Part-time compromise
choices.description: Work weekends only (₹4,000/month), study weekdays. You earn less but protect most of your study time.
choices.consequence_hint: A reasonable middle path, but you still need to find the remaining ₹20,000 somewhere

events.description: Weekends are exhausting but weekdays are productive. You scrape together the rest through small tutoring gigs.

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

rounds.title: Justice vs. Mercy
rounds.situation: {player_name}, you're on the school discipline committee. Aarav, a Class 9 student, stole three library books. The rule is clear: automatic suspension. But you learn Aarav stole them because his family can't afford textbooks and these were his only way to study for exams. He's a first-time offender. His mother works as a domestic helper. Suspension goes on his permanent record.
rounds.story: The rule says punish. Your heart says understand. Both justice and mercy serve a purpose.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian school boy sitting outside principal's office with stolen library books, looking ashamed, discipline committee room visible
rounds.coaching_moment: Mercy without justice is permissiveness. Justice without mercy is cruelty. The challenge is finding where they meet.

choices.label: Follow the rule — suspend him
choices.description: Rules exist for everyone equally. If you make exceptions for sympathetic reasons, where does it end?
choices.consequence_hint: Consistent and fair on paper, but a permanent mark on a struggling student's record feels disproportionate

events.description: Aarav is suspended for a week. His mother takes a day off work to come to school. She loses a day's wages she can't afford.

choices.label: Show mercy — find an alternative consequence
choices.description: Instead of suspension, have Aarav help in the library for a month. Get him a library card. Address the root cause.
choices.consequence_hint: Compassionate and addresses the actual problem, but bends the rules — other students may see it as unfair

events.description: Aarav works in the library every afternoon. He becomes the librarian's favourite helper. He never steals again.

choices.label: Apply the rule but advocate for change
choices.description: Suspend Aarav as the rule requires, but formally propose a policy change: first-time offenders get alternative consequences.
choices.consequence_hint: You follow the system and try to improve it — principled, but Aarav still suffers the current rule

events.description: Aarav is suspended. The policy review begins. Six months later, the rule changes. But Aarav's record still has the suspension.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Rules vs. Compassion
rounds.situation: Your school has a strict no-phone policy — any phone found during school hours is confiscated for a month. {player_name}, during class you notice Priya secretly texting under her desk. You're the class monitor. But you know Priya's mother is in the hospital with a serious illness. Priya is checking for updates. The teacher hasn't noticed yet.
rounds.story: The rule is clear. The context is heartbreaking. What does a good monitor do?
rounds.image_prompt: Indian girl student secretly checking phone under desk in classroom, class monitor noticing, hospital message visible on screen
rounds.coaching_moment: Rules exist to create order. Compassion exists to remind us that order isn't the only thing that matters.
rounds.timer_narrative: The teacher is turning around and might see the phone...

choices.label: Look the other way
choices.description: Pretend you didn't see it. Her mother is in the hospital. Some situations are bigger than school rules.
choices.consequence_hint: Compassionate, but if someone else reports her and the teacher learns you knew, your credibility as monitor is gone

events.description: Priya gets a message: 'Mom is stable.' Relief floods her face. She puts the phone away. Nobody else notices.

choices.label: Report it — rules are rules
choices.description: Tell the teacher. If you don't apply rules consistently, you shouldn't be a monitor.
choices.consequence_hint: Consistent, but Priya might lose her only connection to her sick mother for a month

events.description: The teacher confiscates the phone. Priya's eyes fill with tears. She doesn't speak to you for the rest of the year.

choices.label: Help Priya quietly
choices.description: Whisper to Priya to put the phone away, then ask the teacher if Priya can step out to 'use the restroom.' She can check her phone outside.
choices.consequence_hint: Creative workaround that protects Priya without openly breaking the rule — but you're bending it with a cover story

events.description: Priya slips out, checks her phone, and returns. She squeezes your hand under the desk. 'Thank you.'

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Privacy vs. Safety
rounds.situation: {player_name}, you accidentally see a message on your classmate Rohan's phone while he's showing you a meme. The message, from an unknown number, says: 'Meet me behind the stadium at 8 PM. Bring the money or there will be problems.' Rohan quickly closes it and says, 'It's nothing.' But his hands are shaking. He could be in danger — or in trouble.
rounds.story: His privacy says it's none of your business. His safety says it absolutely is.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian student catching a glimpse of threatening message on classmate's phone, worried expression, school setting
rounds.coaching_moment: Privacy protects autonomy. But when someone might be in danger, respecting their privacy could mean ignoring their safety.
rounds.timer_narrative: It's 6 PM — the meeting is in 2 hours...

choices.label: Tell a trusted teacher immediately
choices.description: Rohan's safety matters more than his privacy. Report what you saw. Let adults handle it.
choices.consequence_hint: You might save Rohan from danger, but he'll feel betrayed — and if it turns out to be nothing, you've violated his trust for nothing

events.description: The teacher intervenes. It turns out Rohan was being extorted by older students. He's furious at you. Then he's grateful.

choices.label: Confront Rohan directly
choices.description: Tell him what you saw. Say, 'That message looked serious. Are you okay? Do you need help?'
choices.consequence_hint: Respects his agency but puts the burden on him to ask for help — he might deny everything

events.description: Rohan denies it at first. Then his face crumbles. 'I owe some guys money from a stupid bet. I don't know what to do.' You help him figure out a plan.

choices.label: Respect his privacy — it's his business
choices.description: He said it's nothing. You're not his parent. Everyone has the right to handle their own problems.
choices.consequence_hint: You respect his autonomy completely, but if something goes wrong tonight, you'll wonder if you could have prevented it

events.description: Rohan goes to the meeting. He comes to school the next day with a bruised arm. He says he fell. You know he didn't.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Tradition vs. Progress
rounds.situation: Your school has celebrated Founder's Day the same way for 40 years — formal assembly, chief guest speech, prize distribution, and a classical music performance. {player_name}, the student council wants to change it: student-led talks, a talent show with hip-hop and beatboxing, and interactive stalls instead of the formal assembly. The alumni association is furious. The principal says, 'It's your call.'
rounds.story: Tradition gives us roots. Progress gives us wings. Can you have both?
rounds.image_prompt: Split image of traditional Indian school assembly on one side and modern student talent show on the other, principal in the middle
rounds.coaching_moment: Honouring the past and embracing the future aren't opposites — but finding the balance requires creativity and courage.
rounds.timer_narrative: The event is in 2 weeks and vendors are waiting for confirmation...

choices.label: Go with the new format
choices.description: It's 2026. Student energy and creativity should drive the event. The alumni will come around.
choices.consequence_hint: Students are thrilled, but alumni donors — who fund scholarships — feel their legacy is being erased

events.description: The talent show is electrifying. Students call it the best Founder's Day ever. Three alumni cancel their scholarship pledges.

choices.label: Keep the traditional format
choices.description: 40 years of tradition deserves respect. The formal ceremony connects current students to the school's history.
choices.consequence_hint: Alumni are pleased, traditions are preserved, but students feel unheard — again

events.description: The ceremony is dignified. Alumni nod approvingly. Half the students are on their phones during the chief guest speech.

choices.label: Blend both — morning traditional, evening modern
choices.description: Formal assembly in the morning for alumni and heritage. Student-led talent show in the evening. Honour both.
choices.consequence_hint: More work, more cost, but both groups feel included — if you can pull off two events in one day

events.description: The morning is respectful. The evening is electric. An alumnus watches the beatbox performance and says, 'I wish we had this in my time.'

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Self-Interest vs. Sacrifice
rounds.situation: {player_name}, you've been selected for a prestigious national quiz competition — your dream opportunity. The competition is on the same day as your younger sister's final board exam. Your parents both work. Your sister has severe anxiety and has asked you to drop her to the exam centre and wait outside. 'I can't do it alone,' she says. No one else is available.
rounds.story: Your dream vs. your sister's need. Your opportunity vs. your responsibility. Both are real.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian teenager holding quiz competition invitation in one hand, younger sister clutching exam hall pass looking scared in the other
rounds.coaching_moment: Sacrifice isn't noble when it's forced. It's noble when you choose it knowing what you're giving up.
rounds.timer_narrative: You need to confirm your quiz participation by tonight...

choices.label: Go to the quiz competition
choices.description: This is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity. Your sister needs to learn to handle things on her own. She'll be fine.
choices.consequence_hint: You pursue your dream, but if your sister panics and performs badly, you'll carry that guilt for years

events.description: You win third place at the quiz. Your sister calls from the exam centre bathroom, crying. A kind invigilator helps her calm down.

choices.label: Drop your sister, skip the quiz
choices.description: Family comes first. There will be other competitions. Your sister needs you today.
choices.consequence_hint: Your sister is calm and performs well, but you watch the quiz results online and see you would have been a strong contender

events.description: Your sister holds your hand during the car ride. She walks in confidently. She scores well. She never forgets what you did.

choices.label: Find a creative solution
choices.description: Ask a trusted neighbour or relative to take your sister. Offer to call her every 30 minutes. Be there in spirit if not in person.
choices.consequence_hint: You try to have both, but your sister specifically asked for YOU — a substitute isn't the same

events.description: Your aunt agrees to take her. Your sister is disappointed but manages. You perform at the quiz but your mind keeps wandering to her.

expert_pick.reason: Goleman's EQ framework rates empathetic responses as the highest-impact leadership move.

rounds.title: Majority vs. Minority Rights
rounds.situation: Your housing society has 50 families. {player_name}, 45 families want to convert the common garden into a parking lot — there's a severe parking shortage. 5 families — including two elderly couples who use the garden daily for their morning walks and one family with a special-needs child who uses the garden for therapy — are against it. The society votes. 45 to 5. The garden should become a parking lot. Right?
rounds.story: Democracy says majority wins. Human rights says some things shouldn't be subject to vote.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian housing society garden with elderly couple walking, children playing, parking lot blueprint overlaid, residents voting in background
rounds.coaching_moment: Democracy is powerful. But a democracy that only counts votes and ignores the most vulnerable people in the room isn't truly democratic.
rounds.timer_narrative: The society meeting is tonight and a decision must be made...

choices.label: Respect the majority vote
choices.description: 45 out of 50 is an overwhelming mandate. The parking problem affects most families. The garden goes.
choices.consequence_hint: Democratic and decisive, but the elderly lose their walking space and the special-needs child loses therapy access

events.description: Construction begins next month. The elderly couple starts walking on the main road. The special-needs child's therapy moves indoors. The parking problem is solved.

choices.label: Protect the minority's needs
choices.description: Some needs are too fundamental to be decided by majority vote. The garden stays. Find parking solutions elsewhere.
choices.consequence_hint: You protect the vulnerable, but 45 families feel their democratic voice was overruled

events.description: The majority is angry: 'What's the point of voting?' But the elderly couple thanks you: 'That garden is all we have.'

choices.label: Propose a compromise
choices.description: Convert half the garden to parking. Keep the other half with walking paths and therapy space. Both sides give up something.
choices.consequence_hint: Neither side is fully happy, but both sides keep something — the art of the possible

events.description: The redesigned space has 20 parking spots and a smaller but beautiful garden. The architect calls it 'the best constraint she's ever worked with.'

expert_pick.reason: The most effective leaders adapt their approach based on the situation — not habit.

rounds.title: Letter of Law vs. Spirit of Law
rounds.situation: {player_name}, final dilemma. Your school's scholarship exam has a rule: 'Only students with 85% or above in Class 9 finals are eligible.' Lakshmi scored 84.8%. She missed the cutoff by 0.2%. She's the first person in her family to reach Class 10. The scholarship would change her life. The committee chair says, 'Rules are rules. 84.8 is not 85.' You're the student representative on the committee.
rounds.story: The letter of the law says no. The spirit of the law — supporting deserving students — says yes. One number separates them.
rounds.image_prompt: Indian girl student's marksheet showing 84.8%, scholarship application form, committee members debating, hopeful student waiting outside
rounds.coaching_moment: Rules create fairness through consistency. But sometimes the most unfair thing you can do is apply a rule without looking at the person in front of you.
rounds.timer_narrative: The scholarship list is being finalized — you have one chance to speak...

choices.label: Argue for Lakshmi — 0.2% shouldn't matter
choices.description: Stand up in the committee and argue that 84.8% is practically 85%, the spirit of the rule supports her, and the scholarship would be life-changing.
choices.consequence_hint: You fight for a deserving student, but if the committee bends for 84.8, what about 84.5? 84? Where's the new line?

events.description: The committee debates for 30 minutes. They grant Lakshmi the scholarship. The next year, three more students with 84+ apply citing this precedent.

choices.label: Uphold the rule — 85% means 85%
choices.description: Rules must be objective. If you bend them for 84.8, the rule becomes meaningless. It's painful but it's fair.
choices.consequence_hint: Consistent and defensible, but Lakshmi — who needed the scholarship most — goes without

events.description: Lakshmi doesn't get the scholarship. Her father works extra shifts to cover her school fees. She scores 92% in Class 10 — without the scholarship.

choices.label: Propose changing the rule for next year
choices.description: Don't break the current rule, but formally propose: 'Scores within 1% of cutoff should trigger a holistic review.' Fix the system for the future.
choices.consequence_hint: Principled and forward-thinking, but it doesn't help Lakshmi right now — she's the one in front of you today

events.description: The committee adopts the new rule for next year. Lakshmi doesn't benefit, but 4 students do the following year. She writes to you: 'Thank you for trying.'

expert_pick.reason: Leadership experts recommend thinking several moves ahead before committing.

coaching_moment: The world's hardest questions aren't between right and wrong — they're between right and right. How you navigate them defines your character.

checkpoints.title: Checkpoint 1: Right vs. Right — 10 Impossible Dilemmas Basics

questions.question: What is 'empathy'?
questions.explanation: Empathy is the ability to understand and share the feelings of others.

questions.question: A good leader should:

choices.text: Listen to the team and consider different views

questions.explanation: Good leaders listen to diverse perspectives before making informed decisions.

questions.question: What does 'delayed gratification' mean?

choices.text: Waiting for a bigger reward instead of taking a smaller one now

questions.explanation: Delayed gratification means resisting a smaller immediate reward for a larger future one.

checkpoints.review_summary: Review the key concepts from the first 5 rounds of Right vs. Right — 10 Impossible Dilemmas. Focus on the core principles and how they connect to real-world applications.

reflection_prompt: Which decision in this run shifted your outcome the most? What signal told you it was the right call?
